title: 12.11.3: Formula Review
originalText:
12.2 Graph Structures

For the Sum of Degrees Theorem, \(sum of the degrees=2×number ofedges\) or \(number of edges=\unsupported{mfrac}{sum of}\frac{degrees}{2}\)

The number of edges in a complete graph with \(n\) vertices is the sum of the whole numbers from 1 to \(n−1\), \(1+2+3+⋯+(n−1)\).

The number of edges in a complete graph with \(n\) vertices is \(1+2+3+⋯+(n−1)=\frac{n(n−1)}{2}\).

12.7 Hamilton Cycles

The number of ways to arrange \(n\) distinct objects is \(n!\).

The number of distinct Hamilton cycles in a complete graph with \(n\) vertices is \((n−1)!\).

12.9 Traveling Salesperson Problem

In a complete graph with \(n\) vertices, the number of distinct Hamilton cycles is \((n−1)!\).

In a complete graph with \(n\) vertices, there are at most \(\frac{(n−1)!}{2}\) different weights of Hamilton cycles.

12.10 Trees

The number of edges in a tree graph with \(n\) vertices is \(n−1\). A connected graph with n vertices and \(n−1\) edges is a tree graph.
